formulas.name: Wave equation (speed, frequency, wavelength)

variables.name: wave speed
variables.description: Speed at which the wave travels.

variables.name: frequency
variables.description: Number of waves passing a point each second.

variables.name: wavelength
variables.description: Distance between neighbouring crests.

formulas.explanation: In one period a wave moves forward by one wavelength. Since f periods fit in each second, the wave travels f λ metres per second. This holds for every kind of wave: sound, light, water and waves on strings.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to convert between frequency and wavelength for any wave whose speed you know.
assumptions: the wave speed is constant in the medium

example.story: A tuning fork sounds the note A at 440 Hz in air where sound travels at 343 m/s. What is the wavelength?

formulas.name: Frequency and period

variables.name: frequency
variables.description: Cycles per second.

variables.name: period
variables.description: Time for one cycle.

formulas.explanation: Frequency counts cycles per second and the period is the time for one cycle, so each is the reciprocal of the other. One hertz is one cycle per second.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for any repeating motion: waves, oscillations, rotations, clock signals and alternating current.

example.story: An oscilloscope shows a signal repeating every 2.5 ms. What is its frequency?

formulas.name: Wave speed on a stretched string

variables.name: wave speed
variables.description: Speed of transverse waves on the string.

variables.name: tension
variables.description: Force stretching the string.

variables.name: linear density
variables.description: Mass per metre of string.

formulas.explanation: A tighter string pulls back harder when displaced, so waves move faster; a heavier string responds more slowly. The speed is the square root of tension over mass per length. Tuning a guitar changes the tension and therefore the speed and pitch.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for guitar, violin and piano strings, and for waves on ropes and cables.

example.story: A string with linear density 0.01 kg/m is under a tension of 100 N. How fast do waves travel along it?

formulas.name: Harmonics of a string or open pipe

variables.name: frequency of harmonic n
variables.description: Frequency of the standing wave.

variables.name: harmonic number
variables.description: 1 for the fundamental, 2 for the second harmonic, and so on.

variables.name: wave speed
variables.description: Speed of waves on the string or in the pipe.

variables.name: length
variables.description: Vibrating length.

formulas.explanation: A string fixed at both ends (or a pipe open at both ends) can only hold standing waves that fit a whole number of half-wavelengths into its length: L = nλ/2. Combining with v = fλ gives the allowed frequencies. The lowest, n = 1, is the fundamental; the others are whole-number multiples.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for stringed instruments, flutes and other open pipes, and standing wave experiments.

example.story: A guitar string vibrates over 0.65 m and waves travel along it at 286 m/s. What is its fundamental frequency?

formulas.name: Harmonics of a pipe closed at one end

variables.name: frequency
variables.description: Frequency of the standing wave.

variables.name: harmonic number
variables.description: An odd number: 1, 3, 5, ...

variables.name: speed of sound
variables.description: Speed of sound in the air inside.

variables.name: pipe length
variables.description: Length of the air column.

formulas.explanation: A closed end must be a node and an open end an antinode, so the pipe holds an odd number of quarter-wavelengths: L = nλ/4 with n odd. Only odd harmonics are present, which gives instruments like the clarinet their hollow tone. The fundamental is half the frequency of an open pipe of the same length.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for clarinets, organ pipes stopped at one end, bottles you blow across, and resonance tube experiments.

example.story: Blowing across a bottle with a 0.25 m air column, what fundamental note do you hear (v = 343 m/s)?

formulas.name: Speed of sound in air and temperature

variables.name: speed of sound
variables.description: Speed of sound in dry air.

variables.name: air temperature
variables.description: Temperature in degrees Celsius.

formulas.explanation: Sound travels faster in warmer air because the molecules move faster. The speed is proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature, and 331.3 m/s is its value at 0 °C. Near room temperature it rises by about 0.6 m/s per degree.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to correct the speed of sound for temperature in echo timing, music and acoustics.
assumptions: dry air treated as an ideal gas

example.story: How fast does sound travel in air at 20 °C?

formulas.name: Doppler effect for sound

variables.name: observed frequency
variables.description: Frequency heard by the observer.

variables.name: source frequency
variables.description: Frequency emitted by the source.

variables.name: speed of sound
variables.description: Speed of sound in the air.

variables.name: observer speed
variables.description: Positive when the observer moves towards the source.

variables.name: source speed
variables.description: Positive when the source moves towards the observer.

formulas.explanation: A source moving towards you squashes the waves in front of it, so the wavelength is shorter and the pitch higher; moving away stretches them. An observer moving towards the source meets the crests more often. Both effects combine in this formula.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for sirens passing by, speed guns, ultrasound blood-flow scans and bat echolocation.
assumptions: speeds much less than the speed of sound
motion along the line joining source and observer
formulas.source: Sign convention: v_o is positive when the observer moves towards the source, v_s is positive when the source moves towards the observer.

example.story: An ambulance siren at 700 Hz approaches a standing pedestrian at 25 m/s. What frequency does the pedestrian hear (v = 343 m/s)?

formulas.name: Doppler shift of light (low speed)

variables.name: wavelength shift
variables.description: Observed minus emitted wavelength; positive is a redshift.

variables.name: emitted wavelength
variables.description: Wavelength measured at rest (in the lab).

variables.name: recession speed
variables.description: Speed away from the observer (negative if approaching).

formulas.explanation: Light from a source moving away is stretched to longer wavelengths (redshift); from a source approaching it is compressed (blueshift). For speeds much less than light, the fractional shift equals v/c. Astronomers use it to measure how fast stars and galaxies move.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for the motion of stars, galaxies, exoplanet wobbles and radar speed measurements.
assumptions: v much less than c (use the relativistic formula otherwise)
motion along the line of sight

example.story: The hydrogen line at 656.28 nm is observed in a galaxy receding at 3.0 × 10⁶ m/s. By how much is it shifted?
steps: Observed at about 662.85 nm, a redshift

formulas.name: Refractive index

variables.name: refractive index
variables.description: How many times slower light travels in the material than in vacuum.

variables.name: speed of light in the material
variables.description: Speed of light inside the material.

formulas.explanation: Light slows down in transparent materials. The refractive index is the ratio of its speed in vacuum to its speed in the material: about 1.0003 for air, 1.33 for water, 1.5 for glass and 2.42 for diamond. A higher index bends light more at a boundary.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the speed of light in a material, or its refractive index from that speed.

example.story: Light travels through a glass block at 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the refractive index of the glass?

formulas.name: Snell's law of refraction

variables.name: first refractive index
variables.description: Refractive index of the medium the light comes from.

variables.name: angle of incidence
variables.description: Angle between the incoming ray and the normal, in radians.

variables.name: second refractive index
variables.description: Refractive index of the medium the light enters.

variables.name: angle of refraction
variables.description: Angle between the refracted ray and the normal, in radians.

formulas.explanation: When light crosses into a material where it travels more slowly, it bends towards the normal; into a faster material it bends away. Snell's law makes this exact: n sin θ is the same on both sides. Angles are measured from the normal, the line at right angles to the surface.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for lenses, prisms, swimming pools that look shallow, optical fibres and rainbows.
assumptions: angles measured from the normal, in radians

example.story: A ray in air (n = 1.00) hits glass (n = 1.50) at 45 degrees to the normal. At what angle does it travel in the glass?

formulas.name: Critical angle for total internal reflection

variables.name: critical angle
variables.description: Smallest angle of incidence for total internal reflection, in radians.

variables.name: outer refractive index
variables.description: Refractive index of the less dense medium outside.

variables.name: inner refractive index
variables.description: Refractive index of the denser medium the light is in.

formulas.explanation: Going from a dense to a less dense medium, light bends away from the normal. At the critical angle the refracted ray would skim along the surface (θ₂ = 90 degrees), and beyond it all the light reflects back. Setting θ₂ = 90 degrees in Snell's law gives this formula.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for optical fibres, diamonds, binocular prisms and why underwater surfaces look silvery.

example.story: What is the critical angle for light going from glass (n = 1.5) into air (n = 1.0)?

formulas.name: Brewster's angle

variables.name: Brewster angle
variables.description: Angle of incidence at which reflected light is fully polarised.

variables.name: second refractive index
variables.description: Refractive index of the medium the light enters.

variables.name: first refractive index
variables.description: Refractive index of the medium the light comes from.

formulas.explanation: At Brewster's angle, the reflected and refracted rays are at right angles. Light polarised in the plane of incidence then cannot reflect at all, so the reflected light is completely polarised. Polarising sunglasses block this glare from water and roads.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for glare reduction, polarisers made of glass plates, and laser windows.

example.story: At what angle of incidence is light reflected from glass (n = 1.5) in air fully polarised?

formulas.name: Thin lens equation

variables.name: focal length
variables.description: Positive for a converging lens, negative for a diverging lens.

variables.name: object distance
variables.description: Distance from the object to the lens.

variables.name: image distance
variables.description: Positive for a real image on the far side, negative for a virtual image.

formulas.explanation: Rays from one point of an object pass through a thin lens and meet again at one point of the image. Similar triangles in the ray diagram lead to this simple relation between the object distance, image distance and focal length. An object inside the focal length gives a negative d_i, meaning a virtual, magnified image (a magnifying glass).
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find where a lens forms an image: cameras, projectors, eyes, glasses and magnifiers.
formulas.source: Real-is-positive convention. Textbooks using the Cartesian convention write 1/f = 1/v - 1/u with u negative for real objects; the results agree.

example.story: An object is 0.30 m from a converging lens of focal length 0.10 m. Where is the image?
steps: d_i = 0.15 m, a real image behind the lens

formulas.name: Magnification

variables.name: magnification
variables.description: How many times larger the image is than the object.

variables.name: image height
variables.description: Height of the image.

variables.name: object height
variables.description: Height of the object.

formulas.explanation: Magnification compares image size with object size. For a thin lens it also equals d_i/d_o, from the same similar triangles that give the lens equation. A magnification above 1 means an enlarged image and below 1 a smaller one.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for microscopes, magnifying glasses, projectors and cameras.
assumptions: sign conventions for inverted images vary; here only sizes are compared

example.story: A 2 cm tall object produces a 6 cm tall image on a screen. What is the magnification?

formulas.name: Power of a lens

variables.name: lens power
variables.description: Optical power in dioptres (1 D = 1 m⁻¹).

variables.name: focal length
variables.description: Focal length in metres (negative for diverging lenses).

formulas.explanation: A strongly converging lens has a short focal length and a large power. Opticians use dioptres, the reciprocal of the focal length in metres. Powers of thin lenses in contact simply add.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for glasses and contact lens prescriptions, and for combining lenses.

example.story: A reading glass lens has a focal length of 0.25 m. What is its power?

formulas.name: Malus's law

variables.name: transmitted intensity
variables.description: Intensity after the polariser.

variables.name: incident intensity
variables.description: Intensity of the polarised light arriving.

variables.name: angle
variables.description: Angle between the light's polarisation and the polariser's axis, in radians.

formulas.explanation: A polariser passes only the part of the electric field along its axis, E cos θ. Intensity goes with the square of the field, giving the cos² θ factor. Crossed polarisers (θ = 90 degrees) block the light completely.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for polarising filters, LCD screens, sunglasses and stress analysis.
assumptions: the incoming light is already polarised

example.story: Polarised light of intensity 100 W/m² meets a polariser at 60 degrees to its polarisation. What intensity gets through?

formulas.name: Diffraction grating equation

variables.name: slit spacing
variables.description: Distance between neighbouring lines (1 divided by lines per metre).

variables.name: angle of the maximum
variables.description: Angle of the bright line from the straight-through direction, in radians.

variables.name: order
variables.description: 0 for straight through, 1 for the first bright line each side, and so on.

variables.name: wavelength
variables.description: Wavelength of the light.

formulas.explanation: Light from neighbouring slits travels paths that differ by d sin θ. When that difference is a whole number of wavelengths, all the waves arrive in step and add to a bright line. Many slits make these lines very sharp, which is why gratings are used to measure wavelengths.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it in spectroscopy, to measure the wavelength of a laser, or to explain the colours on a CD.
assumptions: light falls on the grating at right angles

example.story: Sodium light (589 nm) falls on a grating with 600 lines per mm. At what angle is the first-order maximum?

formulas.name: Young's double slit fringe spacing

variables.name: fringe spacing
variables.description: Distance between neighbouring bright fringes on the screen.

variables.name: wavelength
variables.description: Wavelength of the light.

variables.name: screen distance
variables.description: Distance from the slits to the screen.

variables.name: slit separation
variables.description: Distance between the two slits.

formulas.explanation: Light from two slits interferes: bright fringes appear where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths. For small angles that happens every λL/d along the screen. Young's experiment in 1801 was key evidence that light is a wave.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to measure a wavelength from a double slit pattern, or to predict the fringe pattern.
assumptions: small angles: L much larger than the fringe spacing

example.story: A red laser (633 nm) shines through slits 0.5 mm apart onto a screen 2 m away. How far apart are the bright fringes?

formulas.name: Single slit diffraction minima

variables.name: slit width
variables.description: Width of the single slit.

variables.name: angle of the dark fringe
variables.description: Angle of the n-th dark fringe from the centre, in radians.

variables.name: order of minimum
variables.description: 1 for the first dark fringe either side of centre.

variables.name: wavelength
variables.description: Wavelength of the light.

formulas.explanation: Split the slit into two halves: when light from the top edge travels λ/2 further than light from the middle, every pair of points cancels and the screen is dark. That happens when a sin θ = λ, and again at whole multiples. Narrower slits spread the light more.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for the width of the central diffraction maximum, measuring thin gaps or hairs, and understanding resolution limits.

example.story: A 633 nm laser passes through a slit 0.1 mm wide. At what angle is the first dark fringe?

formulas.name: Rayleigh criterion (angular resolution)

variables.name: smallest resolvable angle
variables.description: Two point sources closer than this angle blur into one.

variables.name: wavelength
variables.description: Wavelength of the light.

variables.name: aperture diameter
variables.description: Diameter of the lens, mirror or pupil.

formulas.explanation: Every circular aperture spreads a point of light into a small disc. Two points can just be told apart when the centre of one disc falls on the first dark ring of the other, at 1.22 λ/D. Bigger telescopes and shorter wavelengths give sharper images.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for the resolving power of telescopes, microscopes, cameras and the eye.

example.story: What is the smallest angle a 10 cm telescope can resolve in green light (550 nm)?

formulas.name: Sound intensity level (decibels)

variables.name: sound level
variables.description: Loudness on the decibel scale.

variables.name: intensity
variables.description: Sound power per square metre.

variables.name: reference intensity
variables.description: Threshold of hearing, 1 × 10⁻¹² W/m².

formulas.explanation: Our ears respond to an enormous range of intensities, so loudness is measured on a logarithmic scale. Every factor of 10 in intensity adds 10 dB, and doubling the intensity adds about 3 dB. 0 dB is the quietest sound a young ear can hear and about 120 dB is painful.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to convert between sound intensity and decibels for noise levels, concerts and hearing protection.
assumptions: I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m² (the standard reference for sound in air)

example.story: A busy street has a sound intensity of 1 × 10⁻⁵ W/m². What is its sound level?

formulas.name: Intensity of a point source (inverse square law)

variables.name: intensity
variables.description: Power per square metre at distance r.

variables.name: source power
variables.description: Total power emitted in all directions.

variables.name: distance
variables.description: Distance from the source.

formulas.explanation: A source that radiates equally in all directions spreads its power over a sphere of area 4πr². Doubling the distance spreads it over four times the area, so the intensity drops to a quarter. The same law holds for light, sound and radiation from point sources.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for loudspeakers, light bulbs, stars and radioactive sources.
assumptions: point source radiating equally in all directions

example.story: A speaker emits 10 W of sound equally in all directions. What is the intensity 5 m away?

formulas.name: Beat frequency

variables.name: beat frequency
variables.description: How many times per second the loudness rises and falls.

variables.name: first frequency
variables.description: Frequency of the first sound.

variables.name: second frequency
variables.description: Frequency of the second sound.

formulas.explanation: Two notes of nearly equal frequency drift in and out of step, so their combined loudness swells and fades. The number of swells per second is the difference between the frequencies. Musicians tune by adjusting until the beats disappear.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for tuning instruments and for measuring small frequency differences.

example.story: A tuning fork at 440 Hz and a guitar string at 444 Hz sound together. How many beats per second are heard?

formulas.name: Photon energy from frequency

variables.name: photon energy
variables.description: Energy carried by one photon.

variables.name: frequency
variables.description: Frequency of the light.

formulas.explanation: Light comes in packets called photons, and each photon's energy is proportional to its frequency. Planck's constant is the proportionality factor. Blue photons carry more energy than red ones, and ultraviolet photons enough to damage skin.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for the photoelectric effect, atomic spectra, solar cells and counting photons in a beam.

example.story: Green light has a frequency of 5.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. What is the energy of one photon?

formulas.name: Photon energy from wavelength

variables.name: photon energy
variables.description: Energy carried by one photon.

variables.name: wavelength
variables.description: Wavelength of the light.

formulas.explanation: Combining E = h f with c = f λ gives E = h c / λ. Shorter wavelengths mean more energetic photons. A handy rule: photon energy in electronvolts is about 1240 divided by the wavelength in nanometres.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when the wavelength is given, as is usual for visible light, lasers and spectral lines.
assumptions: light in vacuum (or air, to good accuracy)

example.story: A blue laser has a wavelength of 450 nm. What is the energy of each photon?

formulas.name: De Broglie wavelength

variables.name: de Broglie wavelength
variables.description: Wavelength associated with the moving particle.

variables.name: mass
variables.description: Mass of the particle.

variables.name: speed
variables.description: Speed of the particle.

formulas.explanation: De Broglie proposed that every moving particle has a wavelength, equal to Planck's constant divided by its momentum. For electrons this wavelength is about the size of atoms, so electrons diffract through crystals. For everyday objects it is far too tiny to notice.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for electron diffraction, electron microscopes and the wave nature of matter.
assumptions: non-relativistic speeds (use relativistic momentum near c)

example.story: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron (9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg) moving at 1.0 × 10⁶ m/s?
steps: λ ≈ 7.27 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, about the spacing of atoms
